newsitem.title: CROATIA: War-crimes team digs mass grave in Croatia.
newsitem.headline: War-crimes team digs mass grave in Croatia.

text.p: War-crimes investigators have started digging and reached the first bodies in a mass grave in a Serb-held enclave of Croatia believed to contain 260 Croats executed in the bitter 1991 Serb-Croat war.
Three senior officers of the former Yugoslav national army are charged with war crimes by The Hague tribunal in connection to the grave in Ovcara, in Eastern Slavonia.

"The exhumation is part of the International War Crimes Tribunal for former Yugoslavia (ICTY) investigation into the events which ocurred in the Vukovar hospital and at Ovcara on November 20, 1991," Clint Williamson, legal adviser overseeing the excavation for the ICTY, told reporters on Thursday.

The U.N. team of forensic scientists, who arrived last Sunday, are clearing top soil in the painstaking process of gathering evidence and exhuming the decomposed bodies, said Dr William Haglund, the chief of the dozen-strong team investigating the grave.
His team has already reached some bodies lying just 30 cm (one foot) below the surface but has not started removing them.
"The grave has not been tampered with since we last inspected it in 1993," Haglund said.
The team will complete its mission in four to six weeks working without local help and under tight U.N. security.
The exhumed remains will be examined and identified at a pathology laboratory in Zagreb, the Croatian capital, he said.
The press is barred from the site to avoid stirring volatile public reaction on the Croat or Serb sides.
Only a British television documentary crew hired by ICTY has access to record the excavation for historical purposes.

U.N. war-crimes prosecutors say Serb forces fighting to thwart Croatia's secession from Yugoslavia massacred the Croats after conquering Vukovar in a notorious three-month siege that reduced the serene Austro-Hungarian town on the Danube River into rubble.

The excavation became possible after Serbs, stunned by the 1995 defeat of fellow rebels in west Croatia by the Croatian army, agreed to hand Eastern Slavonia back to the government after a transitional period under U.N. administration.
The destruction of Vukovar and the purge of Eastern Slavonia's majority Croat community amount to the most bitter grievance held by Croats against Serbs today.
The issue of missing persons, believed to be buried in Ovcara, has been straining relations between Yugoslavia and Croatia which recognized each other last month.

The indictment alleges that when Vukovar fell to JNA troops and Serb irregulars, Serb forces on November 20, 1991, removed some 260 wounded Croat patients, hospital staff, soldiers and political activists from the hospital, Williamson said.
They were taken to a JNA barracks in Vukovar and then transported to a building in Ovcara where they were beaten for several hours.

A few were relased that evening but the remaining men were transported from a hangar in Ovcara to an isolated spot 1 1/2 km (one mile) away. There they were all shot and buried in a mass grave, Williamson said.
JNA officers Mile Mrksic, Miroslav Radic and Veselin Sljivancanin were indicted last November for war crimes and crimes against humanity for the Ovcara massacre.

Belgrade authorities have denied the charges a massacre ever took place and some officials have expressed relief that the investiagtion was underway, "finally to get rid of the stigma over the Serbs."
President Slobodan Milosevic of Serbia has disregarded numerous demands by the ICTY to extradite the three officers.
But recently cooperation between the tribunal and Yugoslavia has improved "tremendously", Williamson said.
